quiz: Think about what each keyword assumes by default when you write no access label at all, for members and for base classes.
Lay out the members one by one: an int must start at an address divisible by 4, and the total size must also be a multiple of 4.
Later objects may depend on earlier ones, so cleanup must not pull the rug out. Which order keeps that safe?
Ask whether the compiler still writes a no-argument constructor for you once you have written any constructor yourself.
Members are initialized in the order they are declared in the class, not the order you list them after the colon.
Which kind of member can never be assigned after it exists, so it must get its value at the moment it is created?
A const member function promises not to change the object, so think about what the hidden object pointer must point to.
A static member function is not called on any particular object, so ask what hidden object pointer it could possibly have.
Ask whether each object needs its own copy of a static variable, or whether all objects share one copy stored elsewhere.
No access word is written before the base name; recall the default base access for the class keyword.
The constructor body may use the base and every member, so they must already exist. Then decide which of those two comes first.
Friendship is a gift given to one named class; ask whether that gift is passed on to children of the friend.
With a member operator your object is always on the left side; check what sits on the left in a print statement.
Recall the rule that if something can be read as a function declaration, the compiler reads it that way.
interview: State the single language difference (default access for members and bases), then the usual convention for when to pick each.
Explain bundling data with operations, protecting invariants in few places, and freedom to change the internal representation later.
Cover construction order (bases, members in declaration order, body), destruction as the exact reverse, and local objects in a scope.
Mention avoiding default-construct-then-assign cost, and members that cannot be assigned: const, references, types with no default constructor.
Describe this as a hidden pointer to the called object, its type in normal and const functions, and why static functions have none.
Explain one shared copy per class, calling without an object, no this pointer, and give uses like instance counters or factories.
Separate declaration from definition of a static member, say where the one definition must go, and mention the C++17 inline option.
Explain how each specifier caps inherited member access, which one models is-a, and what private inheritance is used for.
Show calling the base constructor in the initializer list, note bases build first, and what happens without a default base constructor.
Explain that a same-named derived member hides all base overloads, why lookup stops early, and the using-declaration fix.
Define friend access and its rules (granted, not inherited, not transitive), then argue whether it weakens or supports encapsulation.
Explain that the left operand of a member operator must already be the class type, and the non-member or hidden friend fix.
Explain why each object needs a unique address so the size is not zero, then how an empty base can take no space.
Use static counters updated in every constructor and destructor, and handle copy, move, assignment and thread safety pitfalls.
